content:
Frailty services for older people with arthritis exist in every part of the UK, but they are organised differently in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. In all four nations the usual first step is your GP surgery, which can review your medicines, check for treatable causes of slowing down and refer you to community physiotherapy, occupational therapy or a frailty team where one exists. Social care help at home is assessed by your local council in England, Wales and Scotland, and by your Health and Social Care Trust in Northern Ireland. For urgent advice, use NHS 111 in England, NHS 111 Wales, or NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; Northern Ireland does not have NHS 111, so contact your GP or the GP out-of-hours service. Call 999 in an emergency anywhere in the UK.

This guide explains what frailty services are, who to ask in each nation, and how they fit alongside your arthritis care. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

What frailty means, and why arthritis matters

Frailty is a loss of physical and mental reserve, so that a small illness, a fall or a change in medicines has a bigger effect than it would on someone fitter. It is not the same as getting older, and it can sometimes improve. Arthritis can feed into frailty because painful joints make people move less, and moving less weakens muscles and balance. Clinicians may use tools such as the Clinical Frailty Scale to describe how much help someone needs day to day. A score is a snapshot, not a label for life.

If arthritis pain is the main reason you have slowed down, say so. Better pain control, exercise and the right equipment may help as much as any frailty service.

What frailty services can offer

What is available varies by area, but services commonly include:

  • A medicines review with your GP or a pharmacist, especially if you take several medicines or have had a fall.
  • A comprehensive geriatric assessment, which looks at physical health, mobility, memory, mood, medicines and support at home. See comprehensive geriatric assessment.
  • Community physiotherapy and strength and balance programmes, which have good evidence for reducing falls.
  • Occupational therapy for equipment and changes at home. See waiting for community occupational therapy.
  • Short-term reablement after illness or a hospital stay. See reablement after discharge.
  • Falls services for people who have fallen or are worried about falling.

England

  • Start with your GP surgery. Many practices and community services work together to identify and support people living with frailty, and can refer you on.
  • For help at home, ask your local council's adult social care team for a free care needs assessment under the Care Act 2014. Carers can ask for a carer's assessment.
  • For urgent advice that is not an emergency, use NHS 111 online or phone 111.

Wales

  • Start with your GP surgery, which can refer you to community therapy, falls or older people's services run by your local health board.
  • For help at home, contact your local council's social services for an assessment of your care and support needs. Carers have a right to an assessment too.
  • For urgent advice that is not an emergency, use NHS 111 Wales online or phone 111.

Scotland

  • Start with your GP practice. Community health and social care services are planned by local Health and Social Care Partnerships.
  • For help at home, contact your local council's social work department for a care needs assessment. In Scotland, personal care is free for adults assessed as needing it, though other costs may apply.
  • For urgent advice that is not an emergency, phone NHS 24 on 111. NHS inform has health information for Scotland.

Northern Ireland

  • Start with your GP practice. Health and social care are run together by Health and Social Care Trusts.
  • For help at home, ask your GP or local Trust about a social care assessment. Carers can ask for a carer's assessment.
  • There is no NHS 111 in Northern Ireland. If you need urgent advice when your GP surgery is closed, contact the GP out-of-hours service. See free arthritis support in Northern Ireland.

How frailty services fit with your arthritis care

Frailty services do not replace your rheumatology team, physiotherapist or GP. If you have inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, keep in touch with your rheumatology team about flares and treatment. If you have osteoarthritis, exercise, weight management where relevant and pain relief remain central. Tell each team about the others, and bring a list of your medicines to every appointment.

Making the most of an appointment

  • Write down what has changed recently, such as falls, slower walking, weight loss, memory or mood.
  • Bring all your medicines, including creams and anything bought over the counter.
  • Bring someone who knows you well if you can.
  • Ask for a copy of the plan and who will follow it up.

When to get urgent help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall where you may have hurt your head, neck, back or hip, or cannot get up.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111, NHS 111 Wales, NHS 24 on 111, or your GP or GP out-of-hours service in Northern Ireland) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility over hours or days, or a hot, very swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for unplanned weight loss, repeated falls or a steady decline over weeks.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is there a frailty team in my area?

Services vary. Ask your GP surgery what is available locally and whether you can be referred.

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by their GP and community therapists. If medicines are stacking up, falls are repeating, or memory is changing, ask whether a comprehensive geriatric assessment would help.

Can frailty improve?

Sometimes. Strength and balance exercise, enough protein, a medicines review and treating pain can all help, even if arthritis does not go away.
